title: Holdback Primewave benchmark notes
content:
Goal
- Quick experiments to understand impact of "holdback" priming (what I'm calling PrimeWave) on tail latencies during mixed-priority bursts.
- Specifically: small steady background traffic (best-effort) + short high-priority spikes (latency sensitive). Measure p50/p95/p99 and QPS under several warmup strategies.

Background / motivation
- We see p99 jumps during short bursts even when average cache hit metrics look "okay". Hypothesis: when high-priority requests arrive, the model KV cache and attention warm paths are cold for that priority lane because prior BE (background) traffic pollutes slots. A small intentional holdback/priming for latency-sensitive requests (send X warmup tokens ahead of main prompt) might reduce tail.
- Need empirical data to decide trade-offs: wasted token overhead vs tail latency wins.

Experiment matrix (short)
- Env: single dedicated GPU node (A100-sim), model: rw-instruct-13B-quant (same variant used in prod canary).
- Client harness: redwood-bench v0.9 (rb-run) that simulates two lanes: background (BE) and foreground (FG). BG: steady Poisson arrival, FG: periodic spikes (100 reqs over 3s).
- Key knobs: warmup_tokens (0, 8, 32, 64), holdback_delay_ms (0, 25, 100), prefill_ratio (none vs softfill), concurrency_limit (per-lane) fixed at 16.
- Each run: 10m steady + 2m spike window repeated 6 times; collect per-request latency and qps.

Commands used (notes to self)
- rb-run --scenario holdback-primewave --bg-rate 25 --fg-spike 100x3s --model rw-instruct-13b-q --warmup 32 --holdback 25 --softfill true --outdir /tmp/primewave/r3
- payload: 4-8 token system, 128 output tokens (kept consistent).

Raw observations (selected runs)
1) baseline (warmup=0, holdback=0, softfill=false)
- steady BG qps ~25, FG peak ~33 (due to concurrency limits)
- p50 55ms, p95 220ms, p99 620ms during spikes
- KV cache hit-rate (foreground traces) ~12% at spike start -> climbs after 6s

2) warmup=8, no holdback
- p99 reduced to ~420ms
- token overhead ~8 tokens/request (~6% cost increase)
- foreground kv-hit ~28% at first 2s

3) warmup=32, holdback=25ms, softfill=true
- p50 50ms, p95 140ms, p99 190ms at peak (best run)
- kv-hit ~74% on first FG requests
- throughput similar to baseline (small extra CPU processing for warmup requests)
- token overhead ~32 tokens (~24% cost bump) but effective latency savings for FG

4) warmup=64, holdback=100ms, softfill=true
- marginal additional p99 improvement vs 32 (p99 ~170ms)
- costs scale, and BG lane tail slightly worsens (BG p99 +30ms) likely due to resource stealing for heavy warmups

Representative ASCII timeline (p99 during repeated spikes)
- baseline:   |---^------^-----^---|  (spike p99 peaks: 620ms, 580ms, 640ms)
- warmup32:   |--^--^--^--^--^--|   (spike p99: 190ms, 185ms, 195ms)

Quick numeric summary (avg across 6 spikes)
- baseline (0): p50 53ms, p95 210ms, p99 610ms, cost factor 1.00
- w8: p50 52ms, p95 160ms, p99 420ms, cost factor 1.06
- w32+hold25+softfill: p50 50ms, p95 142ms, p99 190ms, cost factor 1.24
- w64+hold100+softfill: p50 51ms, p95 135ms, p99 170ms, cost factor 1.48

Notes / interpretation
- PrimeWave (warmup + small holdback + softfill) seems to massively increase KV cache warmness for FG lane on first requests and reduces p99 by ~3-4x compared to baseline.
- Diminishing returns after 32 tokens; 64 tokens gives only modest extra tail benefit but noticeably more cost and some BG impact.
- Holdback_delay helps align warmup completion with actual request arrival (avoid wasted prefill if FG delayed). 25ms seems enough in our synthetic pattern. Too long a holdback (100ms) adds complexity and slightly hurts BG.
- Softfill (i.e., allow trimmed warmup to reuse background contexts when possible) reduced BG interference vs brute warmup.

Open questions / risks
- Real-client arrival patterns are noisier; our spike shape is synthetic. Need a run with trace-driven arrivals from prod-traffic-2026-02 (sampled).
- Some models with longer KV chain may need more warmup tokens; 32 might be model-specific.
- Cost accounting: token overhead needs to be amortized against error-rate or SLA penalties for p99 breaches. Finance input required.
- Interaction with batching: warmups might reduce batching efficiency if warmup creates extra micro-requests. Evaluate in batching-enabled runs.

Next steps / TODOs
- [ ] Re-run with prod-trace overlay (use rb-trace --file=samples/prod_jan2026.json) and same knob matrix. (Ravi to help with trace slicing).
- [ ] Add batching knob: batch_timeout 5/10/20ms and see interplay.
- [ ] Small experiment for dynamic warmup: adaptive warmup length based on recent kv-hit for that tenant (sketch: warmup_len = clamp(8..64, f(hit_last_30s))). Put prototype in github branch warmup/adaptive.
- [ ] Calculate break-even cost: what percentile improvement per token paid. Ask finance for average token cost for dedicated instances.
- [ ] Draft a short runbook for SRE: when to enable PrimeWave per-route vs global.

Notes to self (implementation concerns)
- Warmup requests must be annotated so we don't count them as customer billable in metrics (or tag them separately).
- Warmup should be cancellable if slot preempted; otherwise we accumulate useless warmup tokens.
- Ensure privacy: warmup uses synthetic neutral context not real user content.

Slack snippets I will paste to #serving-runtime
- "Ran PrimeWave runs today. Best config: warmup 32 tokens + 25ms holdback + softfill. Reduced FG p99 from ~610ms -> ~190ms. Cost +24%. Will run trace-driven next. PTAL? JIRA-RI-428 for context."

End notes: keeping this as scratchpad; will refine into a proper mini-PRD if trace-driven results align.

-- Sadia K.
